q: What is Amazon CloudFront?

opts.c: A compute service for running containers

exp.a: Amazon RDS is the relational database service, not CloudFront.
exp.b: Correct. Amazon CloudFront is a fast, secure, and programmable Content Delivery Network (CDN) that delivers data, videos, applications, and APIs globally with low latency and high transfer speeds.
exp.c: Amazon ECS/EKS are container services, not CloudFront.
exp.d: Amazon Route 53 is the DNS management service, not CloudFront.

q: How many edge locations does Amazon CloudFront have globally (approximate as of 2024)?

exp.a: CloudFront has far more than 50 edge locations.
exp.b: CloudFront has far more than 100 edge locations.
exp.c: Correct. Amazon CloudFront has 450+ Points of Presence (PoPs) including edge locations and Regional Edge Caches across the globe.
exp.d: CloudFront does not have 1000+ edge locations currently.

q: What is the default TTL (Time to Live) for CloudFront cached objects if no Cache-Control header is specified?

exp.a: The default TTL is not 1 hour.
exp.b: Correct. The default TTL for CloudFront is 24 hours (86,400 seconds) if no Cache-Control or Expires header is specified by the origin.
exp.c: 48 hours is not the default TTL.
exp.d: 7 days is not the default TTL.

q: What is the maximum file size that can be delivered through CloudFront using a single GET request?

exp.a: 5 GB is the limit for S3 single PUT, not CloudFront delivery.
exp.b: 10 GB is not the correct maximum file size for CloudFront.
exp.c: Correct. CloudFront can deliver files up to 20 GB in size using a single GET request.
exp.d: 30 GB exceeds CloudFront's maximum file size for a single GET request.

q: Which of the following can be used as an origin for CloudFront?

exp.a: S3 is a valid origin, but it's not the only one.
exp.b: HTTP servers are valid origins, but not the only option.
exp.c: ALB is a valid origin, but not the only option.
exp.d: Correct. CloudFront supports multiple origin types including S3 buckets, EC2 instances, ALB, and any custom HTTP/HTTPS server.

q: What is the purpose of CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC)?

opts.a: To encrypt data at rest in S3
opts.b: To restrict direct access to S3 and allow access only through CloudFront

exp.a: S3 encryption is managed through S3 settings, not OAC.
exp.b: Correct. OAC ensures that users can only access S3 content through CloudFront, preventing direct access to the S3 bucket.
exp.c: DNS routing is managed by Route 53.
exp.d: API throttling is handled by API Gateway or WAF.

q: What is a CloudFront distribution?

opts.a: A physical server in an AWS data center
opts.b: The configuration that tells CloudFront where to get content and how to serve it

exp.a: A distribution is a configuration, not a physical server.
exp.b: Correct. A CloudFront distribution is the configuration unit that specifies origins, cache behaviors, and delivery settings for your content.
exp.c: A distribution is not an S3 bucket.
exp.d: A distribution is not a VPC component.

q: Which protocol does CloudFront support for communication between viewers and edge locations?

exp.a: CloudFront supports more than just HTTP.
exp.b: CloudFront can serve over HTTP as well, though HTTPS is recommended.
exp.c: Correct. CloudFront supports both HTTP and HTTPS for viewer connections. You can also configure it to redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
exp.d: CloudFront does not support FTP.

q: What is the maximum number of alternate domain names (CNAMEs) you can associate with a single CloudFront distribution?

exp.a: 10 is not the correct limit.
exp.b: 25 is not the correct limit.
exp.c: Correct. You can associate up to 100 alternate domain names (CNAMEs) with a single CloudFront distribution.
exp.d: 200 exceeds the default limit.

q: Which AWS service is used to provision SSL/TLS certificates for use with CloudFront?

exp.a: AWS KMS is for encryption key management, not SSL/TLS certificates.
exp.b: Correct. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) is used to provision, manage, and deploy SSL/TLS certificates for use with CloudFront. Certificates must be in the us-east-1 region.
exp.c: AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets, not SSL certificates for CloudFront.
exp.d: IAM manages access policies, not SSL certificates for CloudFront.

q: In which AWS region must an ACM certificate be created to be used with CloudFront?

exp.a: CloudFront requires the certificate to be in a specific region.
exp.b: us-west-2 is not the required region for CloudFront certificates.
exp.c: Correct. SSL/TLS certificates for CloudFront must be created in the US East (N. Virginia) region (us-east-1).
exp.d: eu-west-1 is not the required region for CloudFront certificates.

q: What is a CloudFront cache behavior?

opts.a: A rule that defines how CloudFront handles requests based on URL path patterns
opts.b: A metric that measures cache hit ratio

exp.a: Correct. Cache behaviors define how CloudFront processes requests for different URL path patterns, including TTL, viewer protocol policy, and allowed HTTP methods.
exp.b: Cache hit ratio is a metric, not a cache behavior.
exp.c: An edge location is a physical infrastructure component.
exp.d: Billing configuration is separate from cache behaviors.

q: What is the default minimum TTL that can be set for a CloudFront distribution?

exp.a: Correct. The minimum TTL can be set to 0 seconds, which means CloudFront will always check with the origin if the content is up to date (using conditional requests like If-Modified-Since).
exp.b: 60 seconds is not the minimum configurable TTL.
exp.c: 300 seconds is not the minimum configurable TTL.
exp.d: 3600 seconds is not the minimum configurable TTL.

q: What is CloudFront geo-restriction used for?

opts.a: To restrict which edge locations are used
opts.b: To allow or block users in specific countries from accessing content
opts.d: To route traffic to the nearest region

exp.a: Geo-restriction doesn't control which edge locations are used.
exp.b: Correct. Geo-restriction (geoblocking) allows you to whitelist or blacklist specific countries from accessing your CloudFront content.
exp.c: Bandwidth limiting is not a function of geo-restriction.
exp.d: Traffic routing is handled by Route 53, not geo-restriction.

q: What is CloudFront signed URL used for?

opts.b: To provide time-limited access to specific content

exp.a: API call signing is handled by AWS Signature Version 4.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront signed URLs provide time-limited and optionally IP-restricted access to specific files, commonly used for paid or private content.
exp.c: Encryption at rest is handled by S3 or KMS.
exp.d: Origin identity is verified through OAC or certificates.

q: What is the difference between CloudFront signed URLs and signed cookies?

opts.a: Signed URLs work for a single file; signed cookies work for multiple files
opts.b: Signed cookies are more secure than signed URLs
opts.c: Signed URLs expire faster than signed cookies

exp.a: Correct. Signed URLs provide access to individual files, while signed cookies provide access to multiple restricted files (e.g., all files in a subscriber area) without requiring URL changes.
exp.b: Both signed URLs and cookies provide similar levels of security.
exp.c: Expiration time is configurable for both.
exp.d: There are clear functional differences between the two.

q: What is a Regional Edge Cache in CloudFront?

opts.a: An edge location that serves a specific country
opts.b: A cache layer between the origin and edge locations that has larger cache capacity
opts.c: A cache in the origin's AWS region
opts.d: A backup edge location for disaster recovery

exp.a: Regional Edge Caches are not country-specific.
exp.b: Correct. Regional Edge Caches sit between edge locations and the origin, have larger cache capacity, and reduce the load on the origin by caching less popular content.
exp.c: Regional Edge Caches are separate from the origin's region.
exp.d: They are not backup locations for DR purposes.

q: How many Regional Edge Cache locations does CloudFront have (approximate)?

exp.a: 5 is too few for CloudFront's Regional Edge Caches.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront has approximately 13 Regional Edge Cache locations globally that sit between the origin and the edge locations.
exp.c: 50 is too many for Regional Edge Caches.
exp.d: 100 is the number closer to edge locations, not Regional Edge Caches.

q: What is CloudFront invalidation?

opts.b: Removing cached objects from edge locations before they expire

exp.a: Invalidation does not delete a distribution.
exp.b: Correct. Invalidation forces CloudFront to remove cached objects from edge locations before their TTL expires, so the next request fetches fresh content from the origin.
exp.c: Certificate revocation is separate from invalidation.
exp.d: Blocking IPs is done through WAF, not invalidation.

q: How many invalidation paths can you submit per month at no additional charge?

exp.a: 100 is not the correct free tier for invalidation paths.
exp.b: 500 is not the correct free tier for invalidation paths.
exp.c: Correct. CloudFront provides 1,000 invalidation paths per month at no additional charge. After that, each path costs $0.005.
exp.d: 10,000 exceeds the free tier for invalidation paths.

q: Which CloudFront feature allows you to run code at edge locations to customize content delivery?

exp.a: CloudFront Functions is one option, but not the only one.
exp.b: Lambda@Edge is one option, but not the only one.
exp.c: Correct. Both CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge allow you to run code at edge locations to customize content delivery, though they differ in capabilities and scale.
exp.d: AWS Step Functions is a workflow orchestration service, not related to edge computing.

q: What is the maximum execution time for CloudFront Functions?

exp.a: Correct. CloudFront Functions are designed to execute in sub-millisecond time (less than 1ms) and handle millions of requests per second for lightweight operations.
exp.b: 5 milliseconds is longer than the CloudFront Functions execution limit.
exp.c: 5 seconds is the limit for Lambda@Edge on viewer events.
exp.d: 30 seconds is the limit for Lambda@Edge on origin events.

q: What is the maximum execution time for Lambda@Edge on origin-facing events (origin request/response)?

exp.a: 5 seconds is the limit for viewer-facing events, not origin events.
exp.b: 15 seconds is not the correct limit.
exp.c: Correct. Lambda@Edge functions triggered by origin request or origin response events can run for up to 30 seconds.
exp.d: 60 seconds exceeds the Lambda@Edge timeout for origin events.

q: What is the maximum execution time for Lambda@Edge on viewer-facing events (viewer request/response)?

exp.a: 1 second is not the correct limit for viewer events.
exp.b: Correct. Lambda@Edge functions triggered by viewer request or viewer response events can run for up to 5 seconds.
exp.c: 15 seconds is not the correct limit.
exp.d: 30 seconds is the limit for origin events, not viewer events.

q: What is the maximum memory for Lambda@Edge functions?

exp.a: 128 MB is the minimum memory, not maximum.
exp.b: 256 MB is not the maximum.
exp.c: 512 MB is not the maximum.
exp.d: Correct. Lambda@Edge functions can use up to 10,240 MB (10 GB) of memory for origin-facing events.

q: What is the maximum package size for CloudFront Functions?

exp.a: 2 KB is too small for CloudFront Functions.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront Functions have a maximum package size of 10 KB.
exp.c: 1 MB is the limit for Lambda@Edge viewer events.
exp.d: 50 MB is the limit for Lambda@Edge origin events.

q: At which CloudFront event types can CloudFront Functions be triggered?

opts.a: Viewer request and viewer response only
opts.b: Origin request and origin response only

exp.a: Correct. CloudFront Functions can only be triggered on viewer request and viewer response events. For origin events, you must use Lambda@Edge.
exp.b: Origin events are only available for Lambda@Edge.
exp.c: CloudFront Functions cannot handle all four event types.
exp.d: CloudFront Functions handle both viewer request and viewer response.

q: Which pricing class in CloudFront includes all edge locations worldwide?

exp.a: Price Class 100 includes only North America and Europe.
exp.b: Price Class 200 includes North America, Europe, Asia, Middle East, and Africa.
exp.c: Correct. Price Class All includes all CloudFront edge locations worldwide for the broadest coverage.
exp.d: There is no 'Price Class Global' in CloudFront.

q: Which regions are included in CloudFront Price Class 100?

exp.a: Correct. Price Class 100 includes only edge locations in North America and Europe, making it the least expensive option.
exp.b: All regions is Price Class All.
exp.c: North America, Europe, and Asia would be closer to Price Class 200.
exp.d: Price Class 100 is not limited to the United States.

q: What is the CloudFront free tier for data transfer out per month?

exp.a: Correct. CloudFront offers 1 TB of data transfer out to the internet per month as part of the always-free tier (not limited to 12 months).
exp.b: 50 GB is not the correct free tier amount.
exp.c: 10 GB is not the correct free tier amount.
exp.d: 100 GB is not the correct free tier amount.

q: How many HTTP/HTTPS requests are included in the CloudFront free tier per month?

exp.a: 1 million is not the correct free tier amount.
exp.b: 2 million is not the correct free tier amount.
exp.c: Correct. CloudFront free tier includes 10,000,000 HTTP/HTTPS requests per month.
exp.d: 100 million exceeds the free tier allowance.

q: What is AWS WAF and how does it relate to CloudFront?

opts.a: A storage service that CloudFront uses for caching
opts.b: A web application firewall that can be attached to CloudFront to protect against web exploits
opts.c: A monitoring tool for CloudFront performance
opts.d: A DNS service for CloudFront routing

exp.a: WAF is not a storage service.
exp.b: Correct. AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) can be associated with CloudFront distributions to filter malicious traffic, block specific IPs, and protect against common web exploits like SQL injection and XSS.
exp.c: CloudWatch is the monitoring tool, not WAF.
exp.d: Route 53 handles DNS, not WAF.

q: Which AWS service is commonly used with CloudFront to route traffic to the distribution using a custom domain?

exp.a: VPC is for networking within AWS, not DNS routing.
exp.b: Correct. Route 53 is used to create DNS records (like CNAME or Alias) that point custom domain names to your CloudFront distribution.
exp.c: Direct Connect is for dedicated network connections, not DNS.
exp.d: SQS is a messaging queue service, unrelated to DNS routing.

q: What type of Route 53 record should you create to point your domain to a CloudFront distribution?

exp.a: MX records are for email routing.
exp.b: Correct. An Alias A record in Route 53 can point directly to a CloudFront distribution, which is more efficient than a CNAME for the zone apex.
exp.c: TXT records are for text verification, not traffic routing.
exp.d: SRV records are for service discovery, not CDN routing.

q: What is CloudFront Origin Shield?

opts.b: An additional caching layer between regional edge caches and the origin to reduce origin load
opts.c: A firewall for the origin server
opts.d: An encryption feature for origin data

exp.a: DDoS protection is provided by AWS Shield, not Origin Shield specifically.
exp.b: Correct. Origin Shield adds a centralized caching layer that reduces the number of requests going to your origin, improving cache hit ratio and reducing origin load.
exp.c: Firewall functionality is provided by WAF or Security Groups.
exp.d: Encryption is handled by SSL/TLS or KMS.

q: Which HTTP methods does CloudFront support?

opts.c: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE

exp.a: CloudFront supports more than just GET and HEAD.
exp.b: CloudFront supports more methods than GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS.
exp.c: Correct. CloudFront supports GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, and DELETE methods. You configure which methods are allowed per cache behavior.
exp.d: CloudFront supports far more than just GET.

q: What is the maximum number of origins you can configure per CloudFront distribution?

exp.a: 10 is not the default limit for origins.
exp.b: Correct. By default, you can have up to 25 origins per CloudFront distribution (can be increased via service quota request).
exp.c: 50 is not the default limit.
exp.d: 100 is not the default limit.

q: What is the maximum number of cache behaviors per CloudFront distribution?

exp.a: 10 is not the default limit.
exp.b: Correct. By default, you can have up to 25 cache behaviors per CloudFront distribution (can be increased).
exp.c: 50 is not the default limit.
exp.d: 100 is not the default limit.

q: What is CloudFront Origin Failover?

opts.a: Automatically switching to a secondary origin when the primary origin returns specific error codes
opts.c: Redirecting users to a different edge location

exp.a: Correct. Origin Failover allows CloudFront to automatically route requests to a secondary origin when the primary origin returns specific HTTP error status codes (e.g., 500, 502, 503, 504).
exp.b: CloudFront does not restart origin servers.
exp.c: Origin failover is about origin switching, not edge location switching.
exp.d: DNS switching is handled by Route 53, not CloudFront failover.

q: What is an Origin Group in CloudFront?

opts.b: A primary and secondary origin configured for failover
opts.c: A group of S3 buckets replicated together

exp.a: Edge locations are not grouped as origin groups.
exp.b: Correct. An Origin Group consists of a primary origin and a secondary origin, enabling automatic failover when the primary origin fails.
exp.c: S3 replication is separate from CloudFront origin groups.
exp.d: Cache behaviors are different from origin groups.

q: Which AWS service provides DDoS protection that is automatically enabled for CloudFront?

exp.a: WAF protects against application-layer attacks but must be explicitly configured.
exp.b: Correct. AWS Shield Standard is automatically enabled at no extra cost for all CloudFront distributions, providing protection against common DDoS attacks.
exp.c: Shield Advanced requires a paid subscription.
exp.d: GuardDuty is a threat detection service, not a DDoS mitigation service.

q: What is CloudFront Field-Level Encryption?

opts.a: Encrypting all traffic between edge and origin
opts.b: Encrypting specific sensitive data fields in POST requests at the edge before forwarding to origin

exp.a: HTTPS handles traffic encryption, not field-level encryption specifically.
exp.b: Correct. Field-Level Encryption allows CloudFront to encrypt specific form fields (like credit card numbers) at the edge using a public key, so only your application with the private key can decrypt them.
exp.c: S3 encryption is managed by S3 settings.
exp.d: DNS encryption is handled by DNSSEC or DoH.

q: What is the purpose of CloudFront real-time logs?

opts.a: To store access logs in S3 for later analysis
opts.b: To deliver detailed log data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams in real time

exp.a: Standard access logs go to S3, but real-time logs use Kinesis.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront real-time logs deliver detailed request-level data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams within seconds, enabling real-time monitoring and analysis.
exp.c: SNS alerts are triggered through CloudWatch Alarms, not real-time logs directly.
exp.d: Billing reports are separate from real-time logs.

q: Where does CloudFront store standard access logs?

exp.a: DynamoDB is not used for CloudFront standard access logs.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront standard access logs are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket that you specify.
exp.c: RDS is not used for log storage.
exp.d: CloudWatch Logs can receive some metrics but standard access logs go to S3.

q: What is the viewer protocol policy 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS' in CloudFront?

opts.b: Automatically redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS
opts.c: Serves content over both HTTP and HTTPS
opts.d: Only allows HTTPS and returns 403 for HTTP

exp.a: Blocking HTTP is the 'HTTPS Only' policy behavior.
exp.b: Correct. The 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS' policy automatically sends a 301 redirect to viewers who connect via HTTP, directing them to the HTTPS version.
exp.c: Serving both is the 'HTTP and HTTPS' policy.
exp.d: 'HTTPS Only' returns 403 for HTTP requests.

q: What is CloudFront Functions' maximum memory allocation?

exp.a: Correct. CloudFront Functions are allocated a maximum of 2 MB of memory, keeping them lightweight for high-scale operations.
exp.b: 10 MB exceeds the CloudFront Functions memory limit.
exp.c: 128 MB is the minimum for Lambda@Edge.
exp.d: 256 MB exceeds CloudFront Functions limits.

q: Which feature of CloudFront allows serving different content based on the device type (mobile, desktop, tablet)?

opts.b: Cache behavior with CloudFront headers for device detection

exp.a: Geo-restriction is for country-based access control.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront can detect the device type and add headers (CloudFront-Is-Mobile-Viewer, CloudFront-Is-Desktop-Viewer, etc.) that you can use to serve different content per device.
exp.c: Origin Shield is for caching optimization.
exp.d: Field-Level Encryption is for data protection.

q: What is the maximum number of CloudFront distributions per AWS account (default limit)?

exp.a: 25 is not the default limit for distributions.
exp.b: 100 is not the default limit for distributions.
exp.c: Correct. The default limit is 200 CloudFront distributions per AWS account, which can be increased by requesting a service quota increase.
exp.d: 500 exceeds the default limit.

q: What does CloudFront use to identify which cache behavior to apply to a request?

exp.a: HTTP method is configured within a cache behavior but doesn't select the behavior.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront matches the request URL against path patterns defined in cache behaviors (e.g., /images/*, /api/*) to determine which behavior to apply.
exp.c: IP address is not used to select cache behaviors.
exp.d: User-Agent header doesn't determine which cache behavior is used.

q: What is S3 Transfer Acceleration and how does it relate to CloudFront?

opts.a: It has no relation to CloudFront
opts.b: It uses CloudFront edge locations to accelerate uploads to S3
opts.c: It replaces CloudFront for S3 content delivery
opts.d: It is a feature within CloudFront

exp.a: S3 Transfer Acceleration is related to CloudFront infrastructure.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront's globally distributed edge locations to accelerate data uploads to S3 buckets over optimized network paths.
exp.c: It does not replace CloudFront; it leverages its infrastructure for uploads.
exp.d: It is an S3 feature that uses CloudFront infrastructure, not a CloudFront feature itself.

q: What happens when a CloudFront edge location doesn't have the requested content (cache miss)?

opts.a: Returns a 404 error to the viewer
opts.b: Forwards the request to the Regional Edge Cache or origin to fetch the content
opts.c: Redirects the viewer to another edge location

exp.a: A cache miss does not result in a 404; CloudFront fetches from origin.
exp.b: Correct. On a cache miss, CloudFront checks the Regional Edge Cache first, and if not found there, forwards the request to the configured origin server.
exp.c: CloudFront does not redirect to other edge locations.
exp.d: CloudFront does not wait to retry; it immediately forwards the request.

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid CloudFront origin type?

exp.a: S3 is a valid CloudFront origin.
exp.b: EC2 instances with public IPs are valid custom origins.
exp.c: Correct. Amazon RDS is a database service and cannot serve HTTP/HTTPS content directly, so it cannot be a CloudFront origin.
exp.d: ELB (ALB/NLB) is a valid custom origin.

q: What is the purpose of the 'Origin Request Policy' in CloudFront?

opts.a: To define which headers, cookies, and query strings are forwarded to the origin
opts.b: To set the TTL for cached content
opts.c: To restrict origin access to CloudFront only
opts.d: To enable HTTPS between CloudFront and origin

exp.a: Correct. An Origin Request Policy controls which headers, cookies, and query strings CloudFront includes when forwarding requests to the origin.
exp.b: TTL is defined in the Cache Policy.
exp.c: Origin access restriction is handled by OAC/OAI.
exp.d: HTTPS between CloudFront and origin is configured in the origin settings.

q: What is the purpose of the 'Cache Policy' in CloudFront?

opts.a: To determine which HTTP methods are allowed
opts.b: To define TTL settings and which values (headers, cookies, query strings) are used as cache keys

exp.a: Allowed HTTP methods are configured in the cache behavior settings.
exp.b: Correct. A Cache Policy defines minimum, maximum, and default TTL values, and specifies which headers, cookies, and query strings are included in the cache key.
exp.c: Origin configuration is separate from cache policies.
exp.d: Geo-restrictions are configured separately.

q: What is CloudFront OAI (Origin Access Identity)?

opts.a: A legacy method to restrict S3 access to CloudFront only

exp.a: Correct. OAI is the legacy method (now replaced by OAC) that creates a special CloudFront identity to restrict S3 bucket access so content can only be accessed through CloudFront.
exp.b: OAI is not an SSL certificate.
exp.c: OAI is not a user authentication method.
exp.d: OAI has nothing to do with logging.

q: What is the maximum TTL that can be set for a CloudFront cache behavior?

exp.a: 24 hours is the default TTL, not the maximum.
exp.b: 7 days is not the maximum TTL.
exp.c: 30 days is not the maximum TTL.
exp.d: Correct. The maximum TTL for CloudFront can be set up to 365 days (31,536,000 seconds).

q: Which CloudFront feature allows you to serve a custom error page when the origin returns an error?

exp.a: Correct. CloudFront Custom Error Response allows you to configure custom error pages (e.g., a friendly 404 page) and optionally change the error code and cache duration for error responses.
exp.b: Origin Shield is a caching layer, not an error handling feature.
exp.c: Cache Policy manages cache settings, not error responses.
exp.d: Origin Request Policy manages what is forwarded to the origin.

q: What are the two types of CloudFront distributions?

exp.a: Correct. Historically, CloudFront had Web distributions (for HTTP/HTTPS content) and RTMP distributions (for streaming media). Note: RTMP distributions are no longer supported for new creation since December 2020.
exp.b: Static and Dynamic are not distribution types.
exp.c: Public and Private are not distribution types.
exp.d: Standard and Premium are not distribution types.

q: What happens if you configure CloudFront to use HTTPS between CloudFront and the origin (origin protocol policy: HTTPS Only)?

opts.a: CloudFront will only connect to the origin using HTTPS
opts.b: CloudFront will redirect origin requests from HTTP to HTTPS
opts.c: The origin doesn't need an SSL certificate
opts.d: Data between viewer and CloudFront will also be HTTPS

exp.a: Correct. When set to HTTPS Only, CloudFront connects to the origin exclusively using HTTPS. The origin must have a valid SSL/TLS certificate.
exp.b: CloudFront doesn't redirect origin connections; it either uses HTTP or HTTPS.
exp.c: The origin needs a valid SSL certificate for HTTPS connections.
exp.d: Viewer-to-CloudFront protocol is configured separately via viewer protocol policy.

q: What is the function of CloudFront's 'Restrict Viewer Access' (using signed URLs or signed cookies)?

opts.b: To require authentication before accessing content

exp.a: Bandwidth limiting is not a function of restrict viewer access.
exp.b: Correct. Restrict Viewer Access ensures that only viewers with valid signed URLs or signed cookies can access the content, providing content access control.
exp.c: Country blocking is handled by geo-restriction.
exp.d: HTTPS enforcement is handled by viewer protocol policy.

q: Which of the following is a use case for CloudFront Functions?

opts.c: Making network calls to external services

exp.a: Correct. CloudFront Functions are ideal for lightweight operations like URL rewrites, header manipulation, redirects, and request/response transformations.
exp.b: Image transformation requires more compute and is better suited for Lambda@Edge.
exp.c: CloudFront Functions cannot make network calls; Lambda@Edge can.
exp.d: CloudFront Functions do not have file system access.

q: How does CloudFront handle WebSocket connections?

opts.d: WebSocket only works with RTMP distributions

exp.a: CloudFront does support WebSocket.
exp.b: Correct. CloudFront natively supports the WebSocket protocol, enabling real-time bidirectional communication between clients and servers.
exp.c: Lambda@Edge is not required for WebSocket support.
exp.d: RTMP distributions are deprecated and unrelated to WebSocket.

q: What is the CloudFront cache hit ratio?

opts.a: The percentage of requests served from the cache without going to the origin
opts.b: The ratio of HTTP to HTTPS requests
opts.c: The percentage of successful vs failed requests
opts.d: The ratio of GET to POST requests

exp.a: Correct. Cache hit ratio measures the percentage of viewer requests that are served directly from the CloudFront cache (edge or regional), without requiring a fetch from the origin.
exp.b: This is not what cache hit ratio measures.
exp.c: Success/failure ratio is different from cache hit ratio.
exp.d: Method ratio is different from cache hit ratio.

q: Which AWS service can you use to monitor CloudFront metrics like requests, bytes downloaded, and error rates?

exp.a: CloudTrail logs API calls, not operational metrics.
exp.b: Correct. Amazon CloudWatch provides metrics for CloudFront including total requests, bytes downloaded/uploaded, error rates, and cache hit ratio.
exp.c: AWS Config tracks configuration changes, not operational metrics.
exp.d: Amazon Inspector is for security vulnerability assessment.

q: What does CloudFront compress content with when compression is enabled?

exp.a: Gzip is one of the supported formats but not the only one.
exp.b: Brotli is one of the supported formats but not the only one.
exp.c: Correct. When compression is enabled, CloudFront can compress content using both Gzip and Brotli formats, depending on what the viewer's Accept-Encoding header supports.
exp.d: ZIP format is not used for HTTP content compression in CloudFront.
